cards.front: Can you instantiate an abstract class?
cards.back: No — new on an abstract class is a compile error
cards.extra: It exists to be extended. Subclasses supply the abstract methods and become concrete.

cards.front: What keyword declares an abstract class or method?
cards.back: abstract
cards.extra: An abstract class may contain both abstract methods (no body) and ordinary methods with bodies.

cards.front: What are Java's four access levels?
cards.back: private, default (package-private), protected, public
cards.extra: Each widens visibility: class only → package → package plus subclasses → everywhere.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::03 Access Modifiers

cards.front: What does the collections framework provide?
cards.back: Reusable interfaces and classes for data structures and algorithms, instead of hand-written ones
cards.extra: List, Set, Queue, Map plus implementations such as ArrayList, HashSet and HashMap.

cards.front: What are the algorithms in the collections framework?
cards.back: Static methods on Collections that operate on collections: sort, shuffle, reverse, binarySearch, min, max
cards.extra: They are generic: the same Collections.sort works on any List with comparable elements.

cards.front: What are Java annotations?
cards.back: Metadata about source code — consumed by the compiler and tools, not executed as program logic
cards.extra: They do not change what the code does by themselves; something must read them.

cards.front: Name the common predefined Java annotations.
cards.back: @Override, @Deprecated, @SuppressWarnings, @FunctionalInterface
cards.extra: Each is checked by the compiler: @Override fails if there is nothing to override, @FunctionalInterface fails with two abstract methods.

cards.front: What is ArrayBlockingQueue?
cards.back: A bounded blocking queue backed by an array
cards.extra: Capacity is fixed at construction, so producers block when it fills — natural back-pressure.

cards.front: What makes a BlockingQueue different from a Queue?
cards.back: Its operations wait until they can succeed: put blocks when full, take when empty
cards.extra: That waiting is the whole point — it replaces hand-written wait/notify between producer and consumer.

cards.front: What is ArrayDeque?
cards.back: A resizable-array implementation of Deque that also implements Queue
cards.extra: It can be used as a stack (faster than Stack) or a queue.

cards.front: What is ArrayList?
cards.back: A resizable array implementation of the List interface
cards.extra: Fast index access, slow middle insertion — the array has to shift.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::02 Array vs ArrayList

cards.front: What is an array?
cards.back: A collection of a fixed number of elements of the same type
cards.extra: The length is set at creation and cannot change; access is by index from 0.

cards.front: Does int[] b = a; copy an array?
cards.back: No — it copies the reference, so both variables point at the same array
cards.extra: Writing through either changes the one array. Use Arrays.copyOf or clone() for a real copy.

cards.front: What is unboxing, and what can it throw?
cards.back: Converting a wrapper back to a primitive; a NullPointerException if the wrapper is null
cards.extra: int x = map.get(k); on a missing key is the classic failure.

cards.front: How many bitwise operators does Java have, and what do they operate on?
cards.back: Seven — on integer types (byte, short, int, long) at the bit level
cards.extra: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>, >>>. They are not for booleans except the first three, which are also logical short-circuit-free forms.

cards.front: What does break do versus continue?
cards.back: break exits the loop; continue skips the rest of the iteration and re-tests the condition
cards.extra: Both act on the innermost loop unless a label is given: break jumps past the closing brace, continue jumps to the update/condition step and the loop carries on.

cards.front: What guarantees does a do...while loop give?
cards.back: The body runs at least once, because the condition is tested after the body
cards.extra: A plain while may run zero times. Use do-while when the first pass must happen.

cards.front: What does the enhanced for loop iterate?
cards.back: Arrays and anything implementing Iterable — one element per pass, no index
cards.extra: You cannot remove elements or know the index; use an explicit iterator or indexed loop when you need either.

cards.front: What internal buffer size does BufferedInputStream use by default?
cards.back: 8192 bytes
cards.extra: It reads a chunk at a time, so the underlying stream is hit far less often. The same default applies to the writer and reader variants.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What default buffer size does BufferedReader use?
cards.back: 8192 characters
cards.extra: Char-based, unlike BufferedInputStream's bytes — the number matches, the unit does not.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What is ByteArrayInputStream for?
cards.back: Reading from a byte array in memory as if it were a stream
cards.extra: Useful when an API demands an InputStream but your data is already a byte[].
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What is the Collection interface?
cards.back: The root interface of the collections framework — extended by List, Set and Queue
cards.extra: It has no direct implementations; you always use one of its subinterfaces or their classes.

cards.front: How is ConcurrentHashMap different from HashMap?
cards.back: It is thread-safe without locking the whole map, so readers and writers can proceed concurrently
cards.extra: HashMap under concurrent writes can corrupt or loop forever; Collections.synchronizedMap locks everything.

cards.front: What does the ConcurrentMap interface add?
cards.back: Atomic compound operations: putIfAbsent, replace, remove(key, value), computeIfAbsent
cards.extra: A synchronized Map makes each call safe but not a check-then-act sequence — these methods close that gap.

cards.front: How are command-line arguments received in Java?
cards.back: As a String[] parameter of main
cards.extra: java Main arg1 arg2 gives args[0] = "arg1". They arrive as strings, already split by the shell.

cards.front: What are the three comment forms in Java?
cards.back: // line, /* */ block, and /** */ Javadoc
cards.extra: Javadoc comments are extracted by the tool into HTML documentation; the other two are ignored.

cards.front: What is a constructor, and how is it named?
cards.back: A special method that runs when an object is created, with the same name as the class and no return type
cards.extra: Not even void. That is how the compiler distinguishes it from a method.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: What is encapsulation?
cards.back: Bundling fields and methods inside a class and hiding the fields behind controlled access
cards.extra: Private fields plus public getters/setters let the class enforce its own invariants.

cards.front: What does an enum constructor do, and what access can it have?
cards.back: Initialises each constant's fields; it is implicitly private
cards.extra: You cannot call it directly — the constants themselves invoke it when the enum class initialises.

cards.front: What is the difference between name() and toString() on an enum?
cards.back: name() is final and returns the constant's identifier; toString() can be overridden
cards.extra: Log-friendly output goes in toString(); name() is what valueOf matches.

cards.front: What is EnumMap?
cards.back: A Map specialised for enum keys, backed by an array indexed by ordinal
cards.extra: Faster and more compact than a HashMap for enum keys, and it iterates in declaration order.
